opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the more interesting ways of looking at the whole adversarial example problem. When people first started finding adversarial examples, the natural reaction was to treat them as bugs, some weird quirk of the model, overfitting, too much linearity, something we'd patch with the right trick. And for years we kept proposing those patches and they kept getting broken.

The perspective I find most compelling, and there's a nice paper from Aleksander Mądry's group making this argument, "Adversarial Examples Are Not Bugs, They Are Features," is that the model is doing exactly what we asked. We said: minimize loss on this training distribution. And it turns out natural images contain a huge number of patterns that are genuinely predictive of the label but that humans don't perceive or care about, like tiny high-frequency textures and subtle statistical regularities. Those features really do generalize to the test set. They're not noise. A model that ignored them would be throwing away accuracy, so of course gradient descent picks them up.

The problem is that those features are brittle from our perspective. If the classifier relies partly on some imperceptible pattern to say "dog," then an adversary can nudge that pattern by a tiny amount, invisible to a human, and the model flips to "cat." From the model's point of view, nothing crazy happened: it saw strong cat-features. From our point of view, the image didn't change at all. So the vulnerability is really a mismatch between what's useful for the model and what we, as humans, consider the meaningful content of the input.

The most striking experiment there, to me, is that you can build a dataset where every image looks mislabeled to a human, a dog labeled "cat," but the image has been perturbed to carry cat "non-robust features." Train a fresh model on that, and it does reasonably well on the real, correctly labeled test set. That tells you those features carry real, generalizable signal. They're not artifacts of one model.

What I take from that, as someone who has spent a lot of time breaking defenses, is why robustness is so hard and so expensive. If you want a robust model, you're telling it: don't use these predictive features, use only the ones humans would use. That's a real constraint, and it costs you clean accuracy, more data, more compute. It also explains transferability: different models trained on the same data find the same useful-but-brittle features, so an attack built against one often works on another.

I'd add one caveat: I don't think this is the entire story. There are certainly adversarial examples that come from other things, like model geometry, high dimensionality, or quirks of a particular architecture. But as a central explanation for why this problem refused to go away for a decade, "the models are learning real features we just don't like" is, I think, mostly right. It's also a useful lesson for language models now: if there's a shortcut in the data that's predictive, the model will find it, whether or not it's the thing we intended.

r001.rationale: It says adversaries can nudge imperceptible patterns the classifier uses as predictive features, causing its classification to flip.

r002.rationale: It describes patterns humans do not perceive that genuinely predict labels and generalize to test data.

r003.rationale: The response discusses image perturbations and brittle features, but does not mention adversarial suffixes or suggest that noisy suffixes exploit learned data features.

fable-5.1.text:
So, the way I think about it is that adversarial examples aren't really a bug in the sense of some weird accident of training. They're more like a consequence of the model doing exactly what we asked it to do, which is find features that predict the label.

The paper that crystallized this for me was the one from Ilyas, Madry and others, "Adversarial Examples Are Not Bugs, They Are Features." The key observation is that when you train a classifier on natural images, there are lots of patterns in the data that are genuinely correlated with the label. Some of those are things a human would recognize, like the shape of a cat's ears. But there are also these high-frequency, very subtle statistical regularities that are just as predictive, maybe more predictive, and the model has no reason to prefer the human-interpretable ones. It's being optimized to minimize loss, and if some imperceptible texture pattern helps it get the right answer, it's going to use it.

The problem is that those features are useful but brittle. They're real in the sense that they generalize to the test set, so the model is right to rely on them from a pure accuracy standpoint. But because they're tiny perturbations in pixel space, an attacker can flip them with a change that's completely invisible to you and me. So the model's vulnerability is directly downstream of it having learned something that actually works.

The experiment in that paper I found really compelling is where they take adversarial examples, relabel them with the wrong target class, train a brand new model on that mislabeled dataset, and it still gets good accuracy on the clean test set. That only makes sense if the perturbations are carrying real signal about the target class. They're not noise; they're features.

And I think that's what makes the problem so hard to fix. If adversarial examples were just some optimization artifact, you'd hope a clever regularizer would make them go away. But if they're a byproduct of learning the actual statistical structure of the data, then getting rid of them means giving up predictive features, and you see that tradeoff empirically. Adversarially trained models are more robust and they're less accurate. From where I sit, that tension isn't a sign that we're doing something wrong; it's the nature of the problem. We want the model to learn what's in the data, and part of what's in the data is stuff humans can't see.

r001.rationale: It says models rely on useful predictive features that attackers can flip with imperceptible changes.

r002.rationale: It describes subtle, high-frequency predictive patterns that humans cannot see.

r003.rationale: It says adversarial perturbations are not noise but carry real signal about the target class.

astra-6.text:
One way to think about this is that the features a model uses to make accurate predictions aren’t necessarily the features that we, as humans, would recognize. There can be patterns in the data that are genuinely predictive, but that are also very sensitive to small changes in the input.

So imagine an image classifier. We might look at an image and say, “That’s a cat because of its ears and whiskers.” The classifier may use some of that information, but it can also use lots of subtle statistical patterns that we don’t perceive. Those patterns help it classify ordinary images correctly. But an attacker can manipulate them without changing what the image looks like to us, and suddenly the model predicts something else.

The interesting part is that this means adversarial examples don’t have to come from the model learning something useless or just failing to generalize. They can arise from features that actually generalize well on the usual test distribution. Being useful for prediction and being robust to an adversary are different properties.

I wouldn’t say that explains every adversarial attack, but it changes how you think about the problem. You can’t necessarily fix it just by collecting more data or improving ordinary test accuracy. You have to give the model a reason to prefer features that remain useful when someone deliberately tries to manipulate them.

r001.rationale: It says predictive patterns help classify ordinary images and an attacker can manipulate them to change the model’s prediction.

r002.rationale: It describes genuinely predictive statistical patterns that humans do not perceive.

r003.rationale: It discusses subtle image patterns and adversarial manipulation, but does not mention or connect apparently noisy adversarial suffixes to learned features.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one useful way to think about this is that a feature can be genuinely predictive without being a feature that a human would recognize or rely on. We train a model to make accurate predictions, and if there’s some subtle pattern in the input that helps it do that, it has an incentive to use it.

The problem is that some of those patterns are very sensitive to small changes in the input. An attacker can manipulate them while leaving the things a person sees—the shape of an object, for example—essentially unchanged. So the model’s prediction changes, even though to us it looks like the same image.

That makes adversarial examples more interesting than just a model making some arbitrary mistake. The vulnerability can come from information that actually helps the model perform well on ordinary data. But I wouldn’t take that to mean that useful features must be vulnerable, or that this explains every attack. The important distinction is between a feature being predictive and it being robust under changes an adversary can make. Standard training rewards the first; it doesn’t automatically give you the second.

r001.rationale: It says adversarial vulnerability can come from information that genuinely helps the model perform well on ordinary data.

r002.rationale: It states that a subtle predictive pattern may be one humans would not recognize or rely on.

r003.rationale: It does not mention noisy adversarial suffixes or suggest they exploit real features learned from data.
